title: What separates good AI games from slop?
author: Loginaut
selftext:
Hi All,

I'm a software engineer and hobbyist developer, and I've been thinking about what exactly makes a game "slop." I use Claude Code at my day job in in robotics, which is a bit closer to gamedev than enterprise apps. Hopefully this is an interesting take.

It seems like "slop" is the new "asset flip" and really just refers to bad games. So how do you avoid making something bad? I think you need two pieces:

* Taste: you need to have played a lot of games so you can evaluate what feels "good" to play. If you're not passionate about games, you're almost certainly making slop.
* Vision: you need a clear understanding of the player experience, and you have to cut anything that doesn't support it. Without this your game will be a mile wide and an inch deep; you're probably making slop.

Both of these are subjective human experiences, so AI isn't really capable of helping you with them. I think this is why game dev is so hard, even if you can offload the art and code to a generative AI model.

I think knowing the fundamentals is also essential to build something that is good and too big to be easily cloned. Just like how AI art has obvious quirks, AI code can get really weird if you don't review what it's doing.

I think understanding game design as a discipline is also critical, because it's how your vision is executed, and directly impacts how good the game is. I wrote a short blog post about the game design of a Snake + Pacman hybrid if you want a little example: [https://karum.dev/2026/11/21/ai-gamedev.html](https://karum.dev/2026/11/21/ai-gamedev.html)

In summary, I don't think AI is tied to slop except in how it empowers unserious developers to churn things out quickly. I'd be interested to hear your takes though, especially if you're primarily using AI for development.

comments.author: intLeon
comments.body: I've been a senior gamedev for more than a decade. I'd say it is vision and a lot of testing. If you can come up with a good formula and generally acceptable aspects (code, art, design, story etc) then it is not slop. Of course some people will have higher standarts with one or many of these aspects but those simply are not your target audience.

replies.author: Loginaut
replies.body: That's a great point, "slop" can mean totally different things if you're targeting Steam vs mobile, for example.

comments.author: Kindly_Life_947
comments.body: you have fun and good time

comments.author: DeanRayGames
comments.body:
I agree with everything you said 100%. But also, taste is subjective. A lot of AI slop is really apparent. But some people "see" the slop "better" once it's been disclosed. That isn't an excuse not to disclose it (I think AI usage should always be open and freely disclosed), but it is a real psychological effect. If you are already primed to dislike AI generated assets, then simply knowing something is AI generated is going to make you see it as slop, no matter its intrinsic asthetic value. Sort of like how expensive wine will taste better if someone knows the price (or if you put an expensive label on cheap wine, it will taste better to them). 

A lot of what people see as "AI Slop" is honestly slop. But a good chunk of it is psychology.

comments.author: ThisGuyCrohns
comments.body: You know when you see it

comments.author: FoodTimely8137
comments.body: This is such a grounded, spot-on take. Comparing 'slop' to the modern equivalent of an 'asset flip' nails the real issue: players don't actually care how a sausage is made—they care whether the final result feels cohesive, intentional, and fun to play

comments.author: Aervale
comments.body:
There's perceived slop and actual slop. Actual slop is pretty objective, it's too simple or too broken to be anything but a tech demo, or generally lacks the required effort for the release stage.

Perceived slop ranges from visually looking uncanny or AI made to people who'll hate it the second they hear any kind of AI touched the game.

comments.author: Dreamt_Up_Games
comments.body: My opinion is that the amazing abilities of AI is really showing how important game design is as a discipline. Many people thing they have great ideas for a game or that designing a fun game is easy but once you get into all the details, the math, balancing, edge cases, UI/UX, FTUE, etc it shows when someone is using AI as a tool to bring the fleshed out design and vision to life vs someone that is just trying to jump on the “Steam Meta” to try to make a quick buck. The recent release of Slotbound on Steam shows that a game created using AI can succeed even with the AI disclosure but the dev spent a long time building the game, gathering feedback, etc. All those posts on social media of “Claude made GTA 6 with one prompt” are leading people to believe that making a good game is easy now. Just my 2 cents :)

replies.author: Loginaut
replies.body:
I have run into this same issue! I cranked through the math and simulation, but the UI/UX has been such a huge pain point. AI had been useful to "brute force it" by generating a bunch of different layouts quickly, but it's a slow and frustrating process. And most of them aren't very good.

I probably need to just pick up a UX book and come back to it later.

replies.author: WetPlug88
replies.body:
Like anything with AI assistance, you need to actually learn about UI/UX design 
You need to look at real actual references of good UI and UX and break them down and analyse why they work
You need to understand it, have a vision, plan it out, and then use the AI tools to make realising your vision take a week instead of 6 months.

That is AIs power and purpose.
It will never make a good UI from vague prompts someone who doesn't know anything about good UI inputs to it.

replies.author: Previous_Host_9990
replies.body:
This was the hardest pill to swallow when AI "unlocked" me to build games... 

I've got a bunch up on Itch.io and several steam pages waiting for demos of games I planned to release. But the more I've practiced the craft and iterated to make games worthy of playing, the more I realized the ideas I thought were so great were really just... Meh. 

And that no idea, great or meh, will be something someone will want to pay for if you don't put a lot of work in, polish, playtest (playtest playtest!) and make the game something that you yourself can happily play for hours and still want more. 

None of this zero-shot nonsense has that. And many (most) human made games also don't have it. 

I think making good games is one of the hardest things I've ever tried to do, and I think it will be the last creative domain to be dominated by "just AI".

replies.author: Dreamt_Up_Games
replies.body: That is a great insight but also don’t go the other extreme and fall into the impostor syndrome trap. If find like the longer I work on a project the more I keep thinking it’s crap and no one wants it. That’s why it’s important to get external feedback early and often. Good luck!

replies.author: Previous_Host_9990
replies.body:
Totally. 

And I think it's part of the process. You have to realize how hard it is or you're just obliviously going to make crap. But you also have to stay excited and keep building...

Not unrelated - if you ever want a playtester or want to playtest... I know a guy / some games!

replies.author: Cosmonan
replies.body: Exactly! I believe the most lacking disciplines now will be related to humanities now: game design, art direction, history and so on.

replies.author: House13Games
replies.body: It's time for the Ideas Guy to shine.

comments.author: PM_Me_Those_
comments.body:
If you have to ask the question then that may already be a sign that you don't have the "eye" for this. Do you know what makes a game fun? Do you know what makes a game visually appealing? Do you even have a vague sense of either? If someone were to hand you an unfinished demo to play, could you pinpoint the small things that make it unfun or unappealing and describe them in excruciating detail? 

If you can't see yourself going through this type of thought process on every single change you make to a project, then you are probably not cut out for it. That's just the honest truth. Your first thought with anything that isn't absolutely perfect should be, "I need to describe this with an embarrassing level of detail so the AI can consider all approaches for a fix."

comments.author: cactudes
comments.body:
AI does not mean slop automatically, except it mostly does. There are a lot of people using AI honestly, but the problem is that there are companies (and people) who generate so much slop that honest work becomes invisible. The worst part are the people who simply ask AI to generate something stupid and then go on the internet "Look what I did", like whatever, anybody with AI and 15 minutes can do it, why do you need to spam it everywhere?

There are some good examples of AI usage, but 99% is slop.

comments.author: DrinkingAtQuarks
comments.body:
For me it's: 

1) Innovation: Slop imitates, it doesn't extend an idea or introduce new ones. It's the same as some existing game but worse.

2) Polish and sparkle. Slop is incomplete, unfinished. Key bindings don't make sense, the UI is clunky etc. Bugs abound. Visually, the lighting or art design is bland or confusing.

3) Balance. The game balance and progression is uneven and unsatifying. Some mechanics are excessively deep, others too shallow.

So by the above metrics, AI use and slop are not necessarily the same thing. Slop is inherently a result of bad and lazy design, both of which are fixable with a good human designer who may or may not be using AI.

replies.author: mrpoopistan
replies.body: Or the increasingly popular version of visual slop: the art design is overblown with sparkles and effects and greebles. Also, the endless stream of cyan, orange, and purple which seem to be AI's only effects colors.

replies.author: Conscious_Leave_1956
replies.body: That's basically most non ai games out there. How many versions of NBA 2k, cod or battlefield or far cry or assassin creed is out there?

comments.author: RockDevLabs
comments.body: I may be biased, but i agree. Look at my game teaser, Beyond the Shallows on youtube. I use AI voicews and UI and images (maps) have been egenrated with AI. I did tell people that I used AI but looks like nobody cared, and on their own nobody even noticed.

comments.author: DaRandomStoner
comments.body: Fun gameplay

comments.author: SerenityScott
comments.body:
I'm just getting into this (using Claude to code my games) vs grinding the old fashion way. It's a hobby, for me... my background is Computer Science, but my profession has taken me to cyber security, and more implementation than any kind of dev work on my own.  
That being said, I have an understanding of the fundamentals... and have been a lifelong computer game player, and TTRPG game designer (for paper and pencil games--I make rules and homebrew my own campaigns).

AI dev makes a lot of things easy. I think the difference between slop and a good game isn't some arcane secret. You still have to grind on the game. You have to have vision, personal standards of what you think is good enough, and then spend time iterating long after the inner child in you think it's cool and finished and ready to show people.

Time and effort. That's it.  Claude takes over the grind of the code itself, and the acceleration in what you can do is geometrically enhanced.  But you still gotta polish polish polish.  And since everyone has access to Claude and friends, then you gotta put in above the new 'median level of effort' in order to stand out from the crowd.

At least, that's my sense of things right now.

comments.author: Halloween_Forever_
comments.body: Ai can generate, but it can't  replace that "feeling". UI/UX learning is needed in everything. [first book](https://www.amazon.com/Design-Everyday-Things-Revised-Expanded-ebook/dp/B00E257T6C/ref=mp_s_a_1_1?adgrpid=175826939025&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.ROml6VaVT-LreMrwfkgU02u0GK8xCtv92dUjk6KlHfxsD467UNPWf1pIQeyIFH6km4I6YJi0x_MUwGLMDB3epoyL0XAJSz5-55kfa0DFyLkY4n4RW7tdQG4Y_9VozYq5cQG4Oq646Go-cJPSLA4RMufiXQRvwyUuS-OiwgGsYaipYCb5n65DuOVV43Ip1E9kqM3UYzQDDwEfulzNSq2GTQ.ntaxIds7YRY8R2DFRuTk8QVuOIYC3QCO92dT5qzmKh0&dib_tag=se&hvadid=778270582749&hvcampaign=22345198252&hvdev=m&hvexpln=68&hvlocphy=9010863&hvnetw=g&hvocijid=12631701056941237032--&hvqmt=e&hvrand=12631701056941237032&hvtargid=kwd-299957662242&hydadcr=15144_13839982&keywords=the+design+of+everyday+things&mcid=24ffdd04179e328bbaaacbeec732f9b2&qid=1795294593&sr=8-1) this book is considered the first steps into ui/ux. After that i would get books specific to your project, engine, coding on ui/ux.

replies.author: Loginaut
replies.body: I've got that book sitting on my shelf right now, I guess I'll move it to the top of my reading list!

replies.author: Halloween_Forever_
replies.body: Most of the book is about the concept of ux. It's fundamentals, but gets you in the mindset, if you want specifically how to use it in your game dev work, you will need something more specific to what you are working with.

replies.author: torpidcerulean
replies.body: I'm learning right now just how important UI/UX is for finding and maintaining the fun. Without guidance, it feels like Claude always pushes new features into a relatively unfun set of menus.

replies.author: Halloween_Forever_
replies.body: Codex was doing the same thing. UX in gaming is very important, the great thing about UX in gaming is that most UX problems don't have to be fixed pre-launch. Find better button placeholder graphics later on? Update 2.0. That is the biggest difference between slop and ai dev, you show up, you fix the problems, you listen to feedback.

replies.author: torpidcerulean
replies.body: It's more that Claude seems to default to just making a menu for everything rather than use real gameplay interactions. I have a ranch/breeding mini game in my current project, and claude's first pass on each part was to add a menu button for selecting each parent, a menu button to release, a menu button to feed, etc.

replies.author: Halloween_Forever_
replies.body: Search game reviews too, games that always got ux complaints and the games that got compliments for the same features, play, play, play. Oh here's a good example - everquest, has so many menus it can block out the entire viewscreen if you open them. People made 3rd party imports to fix it, along with their maps too.

comments.author: teejayaiartdirector
comments.body: Good AI games are made by AI not humans, human slop is the new definition of low quality now! 😂

comments.author: bugnetio
comments.body:
Like many have said, it really comes down to game design decisions (Make any LLM tool you use ask you for YOUR decisions instead of assuming), vision, and then playtesting and polish.

Slop is really just the generic output of a “make me a trading card game” prompt and then releasing it, I can only imagine doing that personally… 

The human quality control, direction and reasoning IS the game truly. The AI just helps you the designer get to the result. But even with how good Opus 5.5 is, it will make silly decisions, or misinterpret angles on assets, or misimport, or have floating items on a map. The critical lens of the human being being applied to game development, to me, separates slop from a real game

comments.author: Physical-Bite-3837
comments.body:
In the words of Shakespeare “This above all: To thine own self be true.”

Make a game YOU would want to play and would be willing to spend money on rather than do things based on what you think others will like. If it is something you’d want to play then chances are there will be other people who will feel the same. But you have to be completely honest with yourself. 

Keep in mind not everyone will like or want to play your game and trying to please everyone is a fool’s errand. There are games people like that I have no interest in and games I love that other people think are stupid. It’s best to go by your own compass rather than try to follow someone else’s.

comments.author: LifeJob3038
comments.body: iterating and testing. lots of it. yeah, even more that that.

comments.author: hikotv
comments.body:
Obviously it is tied to AI through user connection. The base state of AI is more close to slop if you just use it as is, or rather how an individual knows to use it, but not only that, their accumulated expertise outside of AI is considerably more important in reflecting the level of the output.   

Similar to how a drawing is not automatically "art" unless it reaches a certain skill level, as well as the viewer's own level of taste.

With games a lot of it can be hidden through gameplay and other elements as long as it's fun, which is why some slop games can still be successful in their own right.

comments.author: caesium23
comments.body: Exactly the same things that separate anything good from slop, whether AI is involved or not: Skill and effort.

comments.author: advator
comments.body: Effort

comments.author: Professional-Emu4891
comments.body:
Mostly agree, but I'd add one thing from experience: with AI the bottleneck moves from building to cutting. When a feature costs an afternoon instead of two weeks, you build way more of them, and that's where the slop creeps in.

I've been making Arsenal Zero, an idle game, with AI-assisted development (Claude Code) and the most useful thing I did was watch what real players actually do instead of trusting my own taste. I added a radio contact mid-expedition where you had to make a choice, and players just didn't understand it, so it went. I prototyped item durability and dropped it because it was one gauge too many on top of everything else. I even had a whole action scene for the first expedition that got rejected. All of those were "good ideas" that AI made cheap to build, and the game is better without them.

So for me it's taste plus vision like you said, but also data and the discipline to delete stuff you liked building. The AI will never tell you a feature shouldn't exist.

comments.author: NeusomaDev
comments.body:
Yeah, taste and vision, basically.

- Understand your genre enough to know what concepts make it fun and what concepts don't

- Understand how to spec those concepts precisely enough to avoid drift into the median training data version of the concept, which is probably not that fun

- Understand your hook that makes your game stand out from the median training data version of it

Do all of those and you win. Miss any of those and you lose. Simple as.

And yes, AI gets associated with slop because effort was a meaningful barrier to entry for slop before AI. Humanslop has existed in gaming for ages, we just didn't have a need for a whole term for it because effort friction sufficed to gatekeep it. You don't have to make slop with AI though, as many of us are trying to prove, lol.

comments.author: Sirramza
comments.body: An experienced game designer, simple as that

comments.author: CashFirm573
comments.body: Qol, good ui, good foundations, and not a copy of same 5 genre every ai dev seems to think will work, also lot of these games lack the creative eye the amount of mistakes ya can spot and how everyone uses claudes basic graphics it's unreal really.

comments.author: vizyn
comments.body:
The bottom line is there is already a pretty well defined path to successfully creating a game. AI is simply a tool that accelerates quite a few of the processes involved, but it doesn't change what's necessary to be successful.. only how to get there. 

A good game idea that checks all the boxes will be successful whether or not AI is used.

comments.author: McHoff
comments.body: A good game is a good game whether or not it was made with AI. If a game is good you likely can't really tell how much AI is used.

comments.author: Strict_Bench_6264
comments.body: “Playing a lot of games” doesn’t mean you understand games. This is a common trap, that leads to derivative game designs.

comments.author: TopTippityTop
comments.body:
I'm a dev with over 20 yrs of experience. I habe a studio whose games have (combined) sold over 10 million copies worldwide.

In my opinion, it comes down to taste, great game design solutions, the right mix of relatability with novelty.

In essence: great vision, then knowing how to execute, when to pivot; then a whole lot of testing to fine-tune.

In terms of success, none of the above matters if you don't also have some luck (usually by being there at the right time), and have good access to marketing/distribution.

comments.author: abateslop
comments.body:
Taste and vision are great. However I'd add COMMITMENT or whatever you want to call it. 

Because anyone can have taste and vision, but what does it matter if they don't produce anything? Committment means refining and testing to the level that makes you happy. Things don't need to be pixel perfect. But they need to meet your standard. If all you do is delegate QA to AI, then there simply isn't a standard to begin with.
